content.text: This recipe makes 1 roll that serves 2 and takes about 15 minutes.
Tamagoyaki
takes a little practice to roll neatly but the flavour is good from the very first attempt. Work on medium-low heat. Rushing the layers leads to torn omelette and uneven rolling.
A rectangular tamagoyaki pan gives the cleanest shape. A small round frying pan (18 to 20cm) works perfectly well and produces a slightly rounder log. Shape it while still hot using a
makisu
or a piece of cling film.
What you need

items.prepNote: or 45ml water with 1 tsp instant dashi powder

content.text: Method
Crack the eggs into a jug. Add the
dashi
, soy sauce, mirin, and sugar. Beat lightly with chopsticks or a fork until just combined. Do not whisk to a foam.
Heat a small frying pan over medium-low heat. Add a little vegetable oil and wipe around with a folded piece of kitchen paper. The pan should be lightly coated, not pooled with oil.

Pour in one quarter of the egg mixture. Tilt the pan to spread it thinly. When the surface is just set but still slightly wet, roll the omelette away from you using chopsticks or a spatula, starting from the far end. Push the roll to the far side of the pan.
Oil the pan again lightly. Pour in another quarter of the egg mixture, lifting the rolled omelette so the new egg runs underneath it. When just set, roll the new layer back onto the first roll.
Repeat twice more with the remaining egg mixture until all 4 layers are rolled together.
Remove from the pan while still warm. Roll in a
makisu
or cling film. Press gently into a rectangular shape and leave to cool for 3 minutes. Slice into 2cm rounds and serve.

items.cause: The egg layer was too thick or the heat too high, causing the outside to set before the inside.
items.fix: Use medium-low heat. Spread each layer as thinly as possible. Roll while the surface is still just slightly wet in the centre. A torn roll still tastes good. Press it together in the mat.

items.symptom: Tamagoyaki is too sweet or too salty
items.cause: The mirin and soy sauce ratio may not suit your taste.
items.fix: Japanese tamagoyaki ranges from very sweet (dashi-maki style) to barely sweet (Tokyo style). Adjust the mirin and sugar down by half for a more savoury version.

items.cause: The egg was not wet enough when each new layer was added.
items.fix: Each layer must be rolled while still slightly wet so the new egg bonds to it. If the egg is fully set before rolling, it will not stick to the next layer.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Tamagoyaki is eaten throughout Japan at every meal of the day. It appears in bento boxes taken to school and work, at the breakfast table alongside rice and miso soup, and as a sushi topping. Kyoto-style tamagoyaki is thicker and sweeter, eaten as a snack. Tokyo-style is thinner and less sweet. The dish is considered a marker of cooking skill in Japanese homes. A well-made tamagoyaki takes patience and practice.
